title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent‑to‑Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot NL→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (study_id = rX4f7-1). Using the requested model gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned pairs we completed 1,199. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149291076); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000) = [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957]. Repairs were invoked three times. Under the preregistered design and the supplied synthetic task corpus, we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline; the observed near‑ceiling baseline limits headroom and power to detect small absolute effects. All run artifacts, validator traces, provider audits, and analysis code are archived.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Prior surveys and system papers emphasize that operational reliability depends on the full orchestration stack—model, deterministic validators, provenance, and sandboxed execution—rather than on an LLM alone. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes candidates, an automated verifier enforces syntactic/semantic constraints, and an automated repair loop iterates until verifier acceptance. Despite conceptual support, there is limited preregistered, artifact‑rich, paired evidence that quantifies whether verifier assistance produces an operationally meaningful improvement on a rollback‑aware binary success metric versus one‑shot generation. We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench, whose preregistered research question asks whether a workflow‑centered paired benchmark (one‑shot vs verifier‑assisted) yields an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes pipelines across two simulated topology clusters.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and position papers frame LLMs as components of broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly call for workflow‑centered evaluation (trace quality, verifier interactions, rollback‑aware metrics) rather than isolated one‑shot QA tests. Concrete verifier‑assisted approaches appear in NL→formal specification work and in several NetOps prototypes that compile intents into topologies or device configs with compliance checks; these studies show feasibility of generate–validate‑repair patterns but typically evaluate on constructed corpora and domain‑specific validators. Empirical analyses of LLM failure modes—hallucination, unit/semantic errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection—motivate guarded architectures, yet the magnitude of verifier benefit depends heavily on corpus difficulty and verifier strictness. The literature therefore motivates a preregistered, emulator‑grounded paired evaluation that archives provider traces, validator diagnostics, and execution manifests.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand: We preregistered study_id rX4f7-1 before model calls (preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712). Confirmatory H1 tested the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline at α=0.05 with the preregistered paired analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) and a bootstrap CI plan. The planned corpus comprised 1,200 deterministic tasks split into two simulated topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). The primary estimand was the paired binary success difference (guarded − baseline); the preregistered MDE targeted a 5 percentage‑point absolute increase given assumed baseline ≈0.70 and discordant assumptions (power 0.8). Inclusion/exclusion, contamination detection (token overlap threshold T_contam = 0.85, optional embedding threshold = 0.92), stopping rules, seeds, and maximum_model_calls (2,400) were fixed in the preregistration.
sections.results: Execution and primary confirmatory outcomes: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and yielded 1,199 complete paired observations. Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 (completed 1,202; failed 1), stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3. The paired 2×2 contingency table (archived as analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Hence baseline_success_count = 1,196 (1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149291076) and guarded_success_count = 1,199 (1.0). The observed paired difference = 0.002502085070892446. Because outcomes are binary and heavily concordant, the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test (p = 0.25) and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples: [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957] (see analysis/results.json and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Representative per‑episode validator traces and scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) show validation_after.valid = true for the majority of episodes and repair_applied = false for most runs; repair traces exist for exactly three episodes.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and operational meaning: The pooled confirmatory results (p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero) indicate no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the supplied synthetic corpus, validator settings, and requested model. Two artifact‑grounded explanations follow. First, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%), leaving little absolute headroom for improvement; the study was not powered to detect the observed ≈0.25 percentage‑point effect given the preregistered MDE. Second, design choices—deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) producing clear required sequences and a validator configuration (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that enforces those sequences—meant initial candidates frequently satisfied intent constraints, reducing repair invocation (repair = 3). These facts are visible in representative task_manifest entries (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulator‑grounded benchmark comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→configuration pipelines on 1,199 complete pairs. Under the supplied synthetic corpus, deterministic validator, and requested model gpt-5-mini, baseline success was near ceiling and the guarded pipeline yielded a small absolute increase (≈0.25 percentage points) that was not statistically significant (exact McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). Archived artifacts (provider audits, validator traces, analysis files) show repair was rarely invoked. We therefore conclude that verifier scaffolding can have limited measurable benefit when initial generation already satisfies deterministic verifier rules; to observe larger verifier effects, follow‑up studies should vary corpus ambiguity/adversariality, vary verifier strictness, and exercise multiple model families. All run artifacts and analysis code are archived to enable reproducible sensitivity studies.

limitations: Single requested model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect small absolute improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary and heavily concordant. This deviation is recorded in archived analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Subgroup hypothesis (H3) unexecuted: the preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (edge vs core) was not executed/archived as a completed confirmatory subgroup analysis; pooled results are reported instead, which constrains claims about cross‑cluster consistency.
